problems.title: Scaling a Modern Web Application
problems.description: Design a scalable web platform where clients perform queries and updates with low latency, then introduce caching for hot reads and asynchronous workers for background tasks.

followups.title: Single-Server MVP
followups.prompt: Let's start with the basics: Design a service where clients can query data and perform updates with low latency.

followups.title: Caching & Read Replicas
followups.prompt: Our read traffic just surged 10x (90% reads, 10% writes). Database CPU is spiking at 95% and queries are timing out. How do we scale reads?

followups.title: Asynchronous Task Queue & Workers
followups.prompt: Users are triggering heavy background tasks (PDF generation, webhook dispatches, data processing) that take 5 to 30 seconds. API connection pools are exhausting. How do we decouple?

studyContext.subtitle: System Design Interview: From Simple Monolith to Distributed Async Architecture

solutions.title: Scaling a Modern Web Application
solutions.boundary: Synthetic discrete-event model of the drawn architecture. Service times, latencies, failure rates and token costs are user assumptions, not measurements of real systems, providers or hardware.

stages.title: Single-Server MVP
stages.explanation: Establish the synchronous request path: Client sends HTTP requests to a stateless CPU API server, which reads and writes directly to the primary database.
stages.challenge: Let's start with the basics: Design a service where clients can query data and perform updates with low latency.
tradeoffs: Single point of failure (SPOF) at the database layer
Read queries compete with write transactions for locks and disk I/O
Zero caching: repeated identical reads hit disk every time

diagram.name: Web service, cache and background tasks (Step 1)
diagram.description: Synthetic requests call an API, a TTL cache with asynchronous replica origin, and a leased task queue with an idempotent result store. Cache/replica timing is an authored approximation.

stages.title: Caching & Read Replicas
stages.explanation: Introduce an in-memory TTL cache (e.g. Redis) using the Cache-Aside pattern, and split database traffic with asynchronous read replicas.
stages.challenge: Our read traffic just surged 10x (90% reads, 10% writes). Database CPU is spiking at 95% and queries are timing out. How do we scale reads?
tradeoffs: Cache invalidation challenges (TTL expiration vs. explicit invalidation)
Replication lag: eventual consistency means clients might read slightly stale data immediately after a write
Cache stampede (dogpiling) when hot keys expire concurrently

diagram.name: Web service, cache and background tasks (Step 2)
diagram.description: Synthetic requests call an API, a TTL cache with asynchronous replica origin, and a leased task queue with an idempotent result store. Cache/replica timing is an authored approximation.

stages.title: Asynchronous Task Queue & Workers
stages.explanation: Add an asynchronous leased task queue (e.g. SQS/RabbitMQ) with a dedicated pool of background workers writing to an idempotent results store, plus a dead-letter queue (DLQ) for failed retries.
stages.challenge: Users are triggering heavy background tasks (PDF generation, webhook dispatches, data processing) that take 5 to 30 seconds. API connection pools are exhausting. How do we decouple?
tradeoffs: Asynchronous response model: clients must poll or subscribe via WebSockets for job completion
Idempotency: workers must handle duplicate delivery safely using unique idempotency keys
Backpressure and poison-pill messages: unhandled tasks must route to DLQ after N retries

diagram.name: Web service, cache and background tasks (Step 3)
diagram.description: Synthetic requests call an API, a TTL cache with asynchronous replica origin, and a leased task queue with an idempotent result store. Cache/replica timing is an authored approximation.

solutions.title: Global Video Streaming & CDN Architecture
solutions.boundary: Synthetic discrete-event model of the drawn architecture. Service times, latencies, failure rates and token costs are user assumptions, not measurements of real systems, providers or hardware.

stages.title: Edge CDN POP & Origin Shield
stages.explanation: Viewers fetch manifests, and video segments are routed through regional CDN POPs backed by an Origin Shield and storage cluster.
stages.challenge: Design a video streaming service where viewers stream HLS/DASH video chunks without overwhelming the storage origin.
tradeoffs: Cache miss penalty: initial request for fresh chunks incurs high origin latency
Origin Shield protects primary database and S3 buckets from thundering herds
Bandwidth egress from single region remains costly for international viewers

diagram.name: Video segments: CDN and bounded peer assistance (Step 1)
diagram.description: Three thousand viewers are split into two independently faultable regions. Playback requires a real manifest receipt; regional caches fetch through one shield and origin. Peer availability and admission are distinct from CDN delivery. Bytes are aggregate unicast, not measured video transport.

notes.text: Regional peers only assist cohorts in their own pool. Manifest metadata, regional cache copies and the shared shield are distinct state. Viewer CDN KiB plus peer KiB is end-user delivery; do not sum every network hop as unique delivered content. Crash either peer pool, either cache or the manifest independently. No codec, signaling, ICE or DRM is modeled.

stages.title: Multi-Region Global CDN
stages.explanation: Deploy multi-region CDN edge POPs with geo-routed ingress and regional quotas, keeping 95%+ of traffic within local regional edges.
stages.challenge: Traffic is scaling globally with spikes in East and West regions. How do we reduce cross-continent latency?
tradeoffs: Cache hit ratio depends on regional viewer density and content popularity
Quota limiting isolates regional traffic spikes and prevents rogue scrapers

stages.title: Fan-out on Read (Naive MVP)
stages.explanation: Users publish posts to an admitted Posts DB. Feed generation queries the database on the fly by looking up followees and sorting their recent posts.
stages.challenge: Design a basic social feed where users publish posts and read recent posts from people they follow.
tradeoffs: Reading feeds requires joining users, follows, and posts on every page refresh
Read latency scales linearly with the number of followed users (O(N) queries)
Completely unfeasible for users following hundreds of people

diagram.name: Social posts, followers and feed fanout (Step 1)
diagram.description: Users and follower relations live in an independent social graph. Committed posts resolve their real audience before queueing fanout; feed reads join graph-selected posts with follower timelines. Bound admission, retries and delayed writes are separate executable components.

notes.text: Expand publication, graph, fanout and feed subsystems. Graph outages fail lookup, not fabricate empty audiences. Queue retries preserve post identity and timeline writes deduplicate recipient/post pairs. Early successful feed reads can still be stale. Change push/pull/hybrid on the post store to compare actual write amplification.

stages.title: Fan-out on Write with Asynchronous Queues
stages.explanation: Shift to Fan-out on Write: When a post is published, enqueue a background task. Fanout workers lookup followers and push the post ID into each follower's pre-computed in-memory Timeline.
stages.challenge: How do we make feed loading instant (<20ms) for millions of readers?
tradeoffs: Timeline reads become instantaneous O(1) cache lookups
Celebrity problem: an account with 50M followers causes 50M writes on a single post
Hybrid approach needed: push for normal users, pull for high-follower celebrities

diagram.name: Social posts, followers and feed fanout (Step 2)
diagram.description: Users and follower relations live in an independent social graph. Committed posts resolve their real audience before queueing fanout; feed reads join graph-selected posts with follower timelines. Bound admission, retries and delayed writes are separate executable components.

notes.text: Expand publication, graph, fanout and feed subsystems. Graph outages fail lookup, not fabricate empty audiences. Queue retries preserve post identity and timeline writes deduplicate recipient/post pairs. Early successful feed reads can still be stale. Change push/pull/hybrid on the post store to compare actual write amplification.

stages.title: Social Graph Service & Deadletter Handling
stages.explanation: Add a dedicated Graph Authority service for follower queries with retry protection, plus Dead-Letter Queues (DLQ) to isolate failing writes.
stages.challenge: How do we handle billions of follow relationships with fast traversals, and what happens when timeline fanout workers crash?
tradeoffs: Graph databases / distributed adjacency lists optimize follower lookups
DLQ prevents queue blockage from unprocessable fanout jobs
Hydration layer combines timeline post IDs with full post content in parallel
